doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

chapter: Vibes, Bermuda and arriving in Canada
title: Teaching himself vibes by ear and records, and the cost of 78s
summary: Nobody could teach him, so he adapted piano exercises and listened to Hampton, Norvo and others; records were expensive.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Oh I wish there was a picture of you with your bike and your drums and your vibes. Were you playing mostly by ear?
By ear? When you started doing the vibes —

Well yeah. Nobody could teach me. So what I did, I was taking piano lessons, I adopted the right hand of the piano, all the exercises and what-have-you, and basically taught myself by listening to Hampton really. And then when Red came along I listened to Red. And then there was one guy that played, Art Van Damme. He was a good player. I started to get a few of his records, and I think there was a group called the Merry Mac Singers, they had a vibraphone player. It wasn’t very popular. It wasn’t heard that much. And it’s like today is. It’s almost becoming an endangered species, which is unfortunate.
Were records back then a precious commodity? I mean were they precious?

Yeah they were. And they were expensive for a guy like me. The first record I bought was “In the Mood” because it was Glenn Miller which was on whatever it was on, Columbia or RCA, and I couldn’t afford that. I had to buy the English version of it by a band called Joe Walsh, which was a shilling cheaper [scats]. But yeah, I forget how much they cost but if you bought the record you couldn’t take the girl to the movies you know.
You had to have your priorities in order I guess. And they were 78s right?
